title: MLB pitch-rigging trial focuses on cockfighting texts: Code words or legit messages?
content:
NEW YORK — The question of whether indicted Cleveland Guardians closer Emmanuel Clase was discussing cockfighting or using coded language about “chickens” and “roosters” to rig pitches was at issue Friday in federal court. The prosecution and defense presented newly revealed text messages to back their arguments.

References to cockfighting are littered throughout Clase’s text messages. The prosecution alleges the language was used to disguise a pitch-rigging scheme. And his defense has argued he’s actually talking about cockfighting — a practice that both sides acknowledge is prevalent and legal in Clase’s native Dominican Republic.

The government showcased messages between Clase and another liaison of the alleged betting scheme. The messages include multiple uses of the word “Zunino” — a former Guardians catcher whose full name is Mike Zunino. He was behind the plate for several of the allegedly rigged pitches.

While the government is not alleging wrongdoing or participation in the scheme by Zunino, it argued, through prosecutor Rebecca Urquiola’s questioning of an FBI agent, that references to the catcher’s name indicate Clase was talking about pitch rigging, and not about cockfighting.

Defense attorney Lindsay Gerdes subsequently showed numerous text messages, also from 2023, that show Clase actually talking about cockfighting. Those texts included numerous videos of caged chickens, with much of the communication occurring in the same group chat where pitch rigging was allegedly being planned.

Clase, 28, and Luis Ortiz, 27, have been charged with wire fraud conspiracy, honest services wire fraud conspiracy, conspiracy to influence sports contests by bribery and money laundering conspiracy.

Clase, a three-time All-Star, is alleged to have rigged 18 pitches over three seasons. Ortiz is alleged to have rigged two. They are accused of engaging in a pitch-rigging scheme as part of a sports betting conspiracy. A third defendant, Robinson Vasquez, was charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. All three have pleaded not guilty and deny the allegations.

The text messages came into evidence through FBI agent Amy Barnett, who was called by the government as a “publication witness,” meaning she was not involved in any element of the investigation but was authorized to present evidence gathered to the jury.

Many text messages the government showed came from Clase’s phone, and some were from a group chat that also involved Enoc Pena and Arismendy Paca, who are alleged to be the two direct liaisons to the group of bettors involved in the alleged scheme.

On May 30, 2023, Clase texted the group about “the chicks all clucking at each other.” Paca responded that the “second rooster came in with all the heat” after the first rooster was “slower,” as they’d expected. That night, Clase had faced Baltimore Orioles infielder Terrin Vavra. On the first pitch, he threw a slider. The second, a cut fastball. Previously introduced betting activity showed bettors in the scheme losing on the second pitch to Vavra — having wagered Clase would throw a slider.

The government also tried to establish that Paca and Pena were communicating with each other about the bets, which would push back against one of the defense’s main arguments. Defense attorneys have alleged that Pena fabricated the scheme and lied to the network of bettors to sell insider information that he didn’t have.

The text messages between Paca and Pena, however, indicate only that they were communicating about roosters, through allegedly coded language. “Only one rooster,” they texted each other in June 2023, with ambiguous references to “Zunino” that followed. The two also texted about communicating with Clase.

The defense showcased numerous text messages, all from May 2023 — around the time the alleged scheme started — of Clase actually communicating about cockfighting. First, Gerdes attempted to discredit the FBI witness by noting she didn’t participate in the investigation, hadn’t even seen messages potentially favorable to the defense and had mistakenly identified at least one person in the video evidence.

Barnett, through questioning by Gerdes, also acknowledged she wasn’t aware that a person on the text chain in question was Paca’s gamecock handler, and the name of the chat, “Con 20/200,” was a reference to a standard bet on a cockfight.

“I don’t know the context,” Barnett acknowledged in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York in Brooklyn.

The text messages that the defense showed all come from May 6-21, 2023, but they all appeared to be legitimate conversations about cockfighting, with references to strategy about the types of roosters that make good fighters. Clase sent Pena videos of roosters in cages.

The group chat also shared a video of a Spanish-language podcast discussing how there are numerous young baseball players involved in cockfighting, including Clase.

“I like to fight my birds where the real cockfights are,” Clase wrote in a text to Pena.

The government’s redirect was brief but reinforced what it believed to be the key difference between the versions of the same evidence. Urquiola, the government attorney, didn’t dispute that those text messages were referring to legitimate cockfighting, but she appeared to attempt to separate those text messages from those the government presented.

She asked Barnett if the text messages the defense showed had any references to the name “Zunino,” implying that the texts the prosecution focused on were related to rigged baseball pitches.

After Barnett’s testimony, the government called Chris Soriano, the chief compliance officer at Penn Entertainment, previously known as ESPN Bet. His brief testimony largely centered on how betting lines get established, the importance of users signing the company’s Terms of Use and the potential downfalls associated with betting using insider information.

Notably, he said he was unaware if bets on Clase’s pitches ever triggered a report by the company’s security and integrity system. His answer was relevant since, to date, there’s been no evidence presented that explains what triggered the investigation into Ortiz, and, subsequently, Clase, in late June 2025.
